newsitem.title: UK: NASA team working for manned flight to Mars - BBC.
newsitem.headline: NASA team working for manned flight to Mars - BBC.

text.p: The U.S. space agency NASA is working on plans to send six astronauts to Mars within eight years of getting the political go-ahead for a manned mission, the scientist who is running the project said on Friday.

Eric McHenry told the British Broadcasting Company (BBC) that he was put in charge of the work after NASA announced earlier this year that evidence of traces of primitive life had been found in a meteorite from Mars.
McHenry told the BBC's Newsnight programme this was vital because it might prove impossible for robots sent from Earth to answer the key question of whether there was life on Mars.
NASA is due to launch a Pathfinder mission on Monday designed to take a Mars Rover to the planet.

"We believe that there will come a point, and earlier probably than later, in which we will want to send humans to the surface of Mars to extend the scientific investigations that the rovers and robots will have performed," McHenry said.

"Our goal is to do enough technology work that when we are asked to initiate a human programme we could have humans on the surface of Mars within eight years or less," he said in an interview at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.
McHenry, who said he believes low-level microbial life exists below the Martian surface, said humans would be needed if it became necessary to drill to find prove this either way.

"There can be a certain amount of robotic drilling possibly, but when it becomes very extensive, if it goes very far below the surface, we think that we are going to need humans on site to help manage that process," he said.
McHenry said the real challenge was to shave the cost of sending a manned mission to Earth's nearest neighbour in the solar system.
"The world could go to Mars at any time that we decided to go do it. The question is how can we do it for (considerably) less cost than has been predicted...in the past," he said.
Officially, the BBC said, the agency claimed manned flights were not on the agenda and was relying on robots to explore Mars.

But NASA astronaut and moonshot veteran John Young told the programme: "Human beings are great explorers...and it's about time that we started looking around for better ways and making the progress we need to explore the solar system with human beings."
"That's our next goal...not because we want to really, but because we have to."
NASA launched a mission to put a Global Surveyor satellite in orbit round the planet blasted off earlier this month.
